segments.text: Welcome back to basic electronics.
In this lecture we will look at a very useful theorem called the Thevenin's theorem.
We will first try to understand why it is possible to represent a circuit with its Thevenin equivalent form.
We will then look at how to extract the associated parameters namely the Thevenin resistance and the Thevenin voltage.
After that we will consider a couple of examples to illustrate how a circuit can be represented by its Thevenin equivalent.
We will also see how the Thevenin parameters can be extracted graphically.
So, let us get started.
Thevenin's theorem is a very useful and important theorem and particularly in electronic circuits we will find it very useful.
But before we look at the statement of the Thevenin's theorem let us see briefly where it comes from and we will do that with the help of this example.
Here is a circuit to which we have connected a load resistor RL and we are interested in this voltage across RL.
And in particular we want to ask this question how is V related to the circuit parameters?
We begin by assigning node voltages to these various nodes in the circuit with respect to reference node.
So, let us first choose a reference node. We have taken that as the reference node.
So, the node voltage there is 0 volts and with respect to that reference node this voltage at node A is V1.
The node voltage at B is V2 and the voltage at node C is V3.
Now what we will do is write KCL equations in terms of V1, V2 and V3 at these nodes, nodes A, B and C.
And in doing that let us define G1 the conductance as 1 over R1, G2 equal to 1 over R2 etc.
These are our KCL equations. Let us look at KCL at node A that is our node A.
We have three currents entering or leaving node A. There is one current going like that and that is V1 minus V3 divided by R1.
So, that is G1 times V1 minus V3.
